dhpak1.11:1.1: 1.10 The Story about the Pig Butcher Cunda Cundasūkarikavatthu “Here he laments, after death he laments,”
dhpak1.11:1.2: this Dhamma teaching was given by the Teacher while he was in residence at Veḷuvana with reference to Cunda the pig butcher.
dhpak1.11:2.1: It seems that for fifty-five years Cunda made his living by killing pigs which he then either used for food or marketed.
dhpak1.11:2.2: In time [28.226] of famine he would go to the country with his cart filled with rice, {1.126} and return with it filled
dhpak1.11:2.3: with piglets bought in villages for a mere pint-pot or two of rice apiece. Back of his house he had a plot of ground fenced
dhpak1.11:2.4: off as a sort of pigsty, and there he kept his pigs, feeding them all kinds of shrubs and excrement.
dhpak1.11:3.1: Whenever he wanted to kill a pig, he would fasten the pig securely to a post and pound him with a square club to make his
dhpak1.11:3.2: flesh swell plump and tender. Then, forcing open the pig’s jaws and inserting a little wedge in his mouth,
dhpak1.11:3.3: he would pour down his throat boiling hot water from a copper pot. The hot water would penetrate the pig’s belly,
dhpak1.11:3.4: loosening the excrement, and would pass out through the anus, carrying boiling hot excrement with it.
dhpak1.11:3.5: So long as there was even a little excrement left in the pig’s belly, the water would come out stained and turbid;
dhpak1.11:3.6: but as soon as the pig’s belly was clean, the water would come out pure and clear.
dhpak1.11:4.1: Maximum Suffering The rest of the water he would pour over the pig’s back, and the water would peel off the black skin as it ran off.
dhpak1.11:4.2: Then he would singe off the bristles with a torch. Finally, he would cut off the pig’s head with a sharp sword.
dhpak1.11:4.3: As the blood gushed forth, he would catch it in a dish; then he would roast the pig, basting it with the blood he had caught.
dhpak1.11:4.4: Then he would sit down with his son and his wife and eat the pig. Whatever meat was left over, he would sell.
dhpak1.11:4.5: In this way he made a living for fifty-five years. Although the Teacher was in residence at a neighboring monastery,
dhpak1.11:4.6: not on single day did Cunda do him honor by offering him so much as a handful of flowers or a spoonful of rice,
dhpak1.11:4.7: nor did he do a single work of merit besides.
dhpak1.11:5.1: One day he was attacked by a malady, {1.127} and while he yet remained alive, the fire of the Mahā Niraya Hell of Avīci rose up before him.
dhpak1.11:6.1: Consequence Before Death The fire of Avīci is a consuming torment able to destroy the eyes of one who stands a hundred
dhpak1.11:6.2: leagues away and looks at it. Indeed, it has been described in this wise:
dhpak1.11:7.1: The ground there is made of iron it burns with fierce and raging heat, for a hundred leagues on all sides, it spreads and remains all over.
dhpak1.11:8.1: Moreover, the Elder Nāgasena employed the following simile to show how much more intense is its heat than that of ordinary fire:
dhpak1.11:8.2: “Great king, reflect that a rock even as big as a pinnacled mansion goes to destruction in the fire of hell in but an instant.
dhpak1.11:8.3: However, living beings who are reborn there, through the effect of their past deeds, suffer not destruction,
dhpak1.11:8.4: but are as though they reposed in their mothers’ wombs.”
dhpak1.11:9.1: When the torment of the Mahā Niraya Hell of Avīci rose up before the pig butcher Cunda, his mode of behavior was altered
dhpak1.11:9.2: in correspondence with his past deeds. Even as he remained within his house, he began to grunt like a pig and to crawl
dhpak1.11:9.3: about on his hands and knees, first to the front of the house and then to the rear. The men of his household overpowered
dhpak1.11:9.4: him and gagged him. But in spite of all they did, since it is impossible for anyone to prevent a man’s past deeds from bearing fruit,
dhpak1.11:9.5: he kept crawling back and forth, grunting like a pig continually.
dhpak1.11:10.1: Not a person was able to sleep in the seven houses round about. The members of his own household, terrified by the fear of death,
dhpak1.11:10.2: unable otherwise to prevent him from going out, barricaded the doors of the house that he might not be able to go out,
dhpak1.11:10.3: but might be confined within. Having done so, they surrounded the house and stood on guard. Back and forth for seven days
dhpak1.11:10.4: crawled Cunda within his house, suffering the torment of Niraya Hell, grunting and squealing like a pig.
dhpak1.11:10.5: Having thus crawled about for a period of seven days, he died on the eighth and was reborn in the Mahā Niraya Hell of Avīci.
dhpak1.11:11.1: The Mahā Niraya Hell of Avīci is to be described in the terms of the Devadūta Discourse.
dhpak1.11:12.1: The wardens of hell punish them with the five-fold crucifixion. They drive red-hot stakes through the hands and feet,
dhpak1.11:12.2: and another in the middle of the chest. And there
dhpak1.11:12.3: they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings—but they don’t die
dhpak1.11:12.4: until that bad deed is eliminated.
dhpak1.11:13.1: The wardens of hell throw them down and hack them with axes …
dhpak1.11:14.1: They hang them upside-down and hack them with hatchets …
dhpak1.11:15.1: They harness them to a chariot, and drive them back and forth across burning ground, blazing and glowing …
dhpak1.11:16.1: They make them climb up and down a huge mountain of burning coals, blazing and glowing …
dhpak1.11:17.1: The wardens of hell turn them upside down and throw them in a red-hot copper pot, burning, blazing, and glowing.
dhpak1.11:17.2: There they’re seared in boiling scum, and they’re swept up and down and round and round. And there they suffer painful,
dhpak1.11:17.3: sharp, severe, acute feelings—but they don’t die until that bad deed
dhpak1.11:17.4: is eliminated. The wardens of hell toss them into the Great Hell.
dhpak1.11:18.1: Some bhikkhus who passed the door of his house {1.128} heard the noise, and thinking it was merely the noise of the grunting
dhpak1.11:18.2: and squealing of pigs, went on to the monastery, seated themselves in the presence of the Teacher, and said to him:
dhpak1.11:18.3: “Venerable Sir, for seven days the door of Cunda the pig butcher’s house has been closed, and for seven days the killing
dhpak1.11:18.4: of pigs has gone on; doubtless he intends to give some entertainment. Think, venerable Sir, how many pigs he has killed!
dhpak1.11:18.5: Evidently he has not single thought of loving-kindness and lacks utterly the sentiment of compassion.
dhpak1.11:18.6: So cruel and savage a being has never been known before.”
dhpak1.11:19.1: The Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, he has not been killing pigs these seven days. Retribution in harmony with his past deeds has overtaken him.
dhpak1.11:19.2: Even while he yet remained alive, the torment of the Mahā Niraya Hell of Avīci rose up before him.
dhpak1.11:19.3: By reason of this torment he crawled here and there in his house for seven days, grunting and squealing like a pig.
dhpak1.11:19.4: Today he died, and was reborn in Avīci.”
dhpak1.11:20.1: When the Teacher had thus spoken, the bhikkhus said: “Venerable Sir, having suffered thus here in this world,
dhpak1.11:20.2: he went again to a place of suffering [28.228] and was there reborn.” – “Yes, bhikkhus,” replied the Teacher.
dhpak1.11:20.3: “He that is heedless, be he lay disciple or one gone forth, suffers in both places equally.” So saying, he pronounced the following verse:
dhpak1.11:21.1: 15. Idha socati, pecca socati, pāpakārī ubhayattha socati, so socati, so vihaññati, disvā kammakiliṭṭham-attano.
dhpak1.11:22.1: Here he laments, after death he laments, the wicked one laments in both places, he laments and he suffers vexation, seeing the defilement of his own deeds.
dhpak1.11:23.1: At the conclusion of the verse many became Stream-enterers and so on, and benefit arose to many people from the Dhamma teaching.
